media:group.media:title: Towards Solar Fuels and Fertilisers
media:group.media:description:
Join us for an exciting discussion on how solar energy could power the future of fuels and fertilisers! Life runs on electrons and protons. Together, or as hydrogen-atom equivalents, they allow plants to store solar energy, underpin the fuels that power society, and help make the fertilisers needed to sustain life.
Simply put, hydrogen atoms decorate many of the key molecular building blocks of our world. Chemists would like to harness this same basic currency to make fuels, fertilisers, and other useful molecules using renewable electricity or light.
The challenge is control. Protons and electrons readily combine to make hydrogen gas, often more easily than they can be directed toward other molecules. Learning how to steer them selectively is therefore a central problem in modern catalysis.
Professor Peters' laboratory is developing new strategies to control this proton-and-electron currency using catalysts, electricity, and light. In this lecture, you will gain an understanding of the broader vision behind this work, emphasising one particularly demanding and consequential reaction: converting nitrogen from the air into ammonia.
We run our annual Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson lecture in honour of Professor Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson– a notable English chemist whose academic and subsequent professional career with Imperial spanned six decades. Through this high-profile lecture series, each year, distinguished speakers discuss cutting-edge developments in the field of chemistry.

entry.title: Seeing signalling: cells, receptors, and metabolism

media:group.media:title: Seeing signalling: cells, receptors, and metabolism
media:group.media:description:

Professor Alejandra Tomas Catala, Professor of Cell Biology, reveals how new technologies are helping us understand the signals that regulate metabolism, and what they could mean for tackling diseases such as diabetes. #ImperialInaugurals

entry.title: Does smoking make you more social? | Research at Imperial

media:group.media:title: Does smoking make you more social? | Research at Imperial
media:group.media:description:
Does smoking really bring people together, or could it be linked to increased loneliness and social isolation?
Dr Keir Philip from the National Heart and Lung Institute at Imperial College London explores the relationship between smoking and loneliness among older adults across Europe. In this video, he discusses the study’s findings and what they reveal about the social impact of smoking.
Imperial’s National Heart and Lung Institute is home to leading expertise in respiratory research. Study with us to learn from global experts and contribute to research with real-world impact: https://www.imperial.ac.uk/nhli/study/

media:group.media:title: Inaugural of Tom Ellis
media:group.media:description: In his inaugural lecture, Professor Tom Ellis explores how synthetic biology is allowing researchers to rewrite DNA and programme microbes to grow sustainable materials. Living Code, Living Materials looks at the emerging field of Engineered Living Materials, including the use of engineered cells to create sustainable fabrics, functional bio-composites and self-repairing materials. Professor Ellis also considers how programming nature could support more sustainable approaches to manufacturing, food production and infrastructure. Professor Tom Ellis is Professor of Synthetic Genome Engineering in the Department of Bioengineering at Imperial College London. His research focuses on synthetic biology, genome engineering, and developing biological systems to address challenges in health, sustainability, and manufacturing. Recorded at Imperial College London on 4 November 2026 as part of Imperial’s Inaugural Lecture series.

entry.title: Cracking the code: targeting HTLV integration to eradicate infection

media:group.media:title: Cracking the code: targeting HTLV integration to eradicate infection
media:group.media:description:
HTLV affects an estimated 10 million people worldwide, yet remains one of the world’s most neglected viruses. Once it infects a cell, the virus becomes part of its DNA, allowing the infection to persist for life.
Join Professor Goedele Maertens, Professor of Retrovirology, to explore how HTLV establishes infection and how existing HIV drugs could offer a promising way to prevent transmission. #ImperialInaugurals

entry.title: How to improve tuberculosis and chronic lung disease care in Africa | Research at Imperial

media:group.media:title: How to improve tuberculosis and chronic lung disease care in Africa | Research at Imperial
media:group.media:description:
How can health systems better support people living with tuberculosis (TB) and chronic lung disease? In this video, Dr Jamilah Meghji from Imperial College London discusses her international collaborative research into integrating TB and respiratory care across urban settings in Africa, with the aim of improving patient outcomes and making care more effective for health systems.
